capture.final_message:
Split the conjunction and use prime-factor decompositions in both parts.

- For \(n\neq 0\), every divisor \(d\mid n\) is uniquely determined by exponents
  \[
  0\le k_p\le v_p(n)
  \]
  for each \(p\in n.\mathrm{primeFactors}\). Thus summing \(d=\prod_p p^{k_p}\) over all divisors factors as
  \[
  \sum_{d\mid n} d
  =\prod_{p\mid n}\sum_{k=0}^{v_p(n)}p^k.
  \]
  Organize this via the standard divisor/factorization lemmas, or an induction on the prime factorization.

- For the second statement, interpret arithmetic-function multiplication as Dirichlet convolution:
  \[
  (f*g)(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}f(d)g(n/d).
  \]
  Since \(n\) is squarefree, each divisor corresponds to a subset of its prime factors, with the complementary subset representing \(n/d\). Multiplicativity then rewrites each summand as a product choosing, independently for every \(p\mid n\), either \(f(p)\) or \(g(p)\). Expanding these choices gives
  \[
  (f*g)(n)=\prod_{p\mid n}\bigl(f(p)+g(p)\bigr),
  \]
  exactly `prodPrimeFactors (f + g) n`.

The essential hypotheses are \(n\neq0\) in the first part, so its finite prime factorization parametrizes divisors, and squarefreeness in the second, so each prime is assigned wholly to one side of the convolution rather than requiring higher-power local terms.
